prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its active form that made incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize on B019 with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. Having read the full first-round exchange, I find the scientific case stronger, not weaker, because no one challenged its maturity or its consequence. The chain from proglucagon processing and the incretin effect, through the active truncated peptide and its islet, gut and appetite actions, to receptor biology and then drugs, has been independently confirmed in large outcome trials with benefits beyond glycaemia. The three names cover distinct, non-overlapping parts of the discovery side: human physiology and secretion (Holst), GLP-1 and GLP-2 biology and receptor action (Drucker), and the active peptide form (Mojsov). A single part fits the three-person cap cleanly. Adding a second part would force one of the three out for no gain in scientific accuracy. I also think the unanimity should not be read as lack of scrutiny; the chair is right that it can hide differing views on discovery versus development, so I state my own view explicitly below.
statement.case_against: Credit is the real weakness, and I do not want to understate it. Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1(7-36/37) form relative to Habener's group is contested, Habener is outside the credited names, and none of us can verify that history from the supplied record. Knudsen is excluded by the cap, and her acylated analogue design is the step that turned a hormone into a once-weekly medicine, so a discovery-centred prize can be read as passing over the people who delivered the patient benefit. I accept that this exclusion is a deliberate judgment and not an oversight. Long-term safety, including in pregnancy and young patients, is still accumulating, though it does not alter the core discovery.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius argues that Knudsen's liraglutide and semaglutide design is arguably as decisive for patients as the physiology, and that the citation should say the physiology enabled the therapies without claiming the drugs.
responses.response: I agree with her citation framing and have adopted it: my citation says the discoveries made the therapies possible, which credits the chain without awarding the drug design. I still do not put Knudsen in the laureate list. Her work is a scientific advance in its own right, but the Committee's question in a capped prize is which contributions established the biology that the therapies depend on, and Holst, Drucker and Mojsov did that. I hold one condition firmly. If the committee reviews the record and finds Mojsov's priority for the active peptide cannot be supported, Knudsen is the natural third name, because the prize would then still contain an identifiable discovery-to-drug link. I would not extend the substitution beyond that.

responses.point: El-Manira says the third place is a real choice between Mojsov and Knudsen, and names Holst and Drucker as a fallback pair if Mojsov's priority cannot be supported.
responses.response: I accept his framing of the third place as a genuine choice. Where I differ is on the fallback: if Mojsov's claim fails, I would prefer Holst, Drucker and Knudsen over a bare pair, because the active-peptide step is then no longer represented among the laureates and the citation would otherwise lose its link to the drugs. A Holst and Drucker pair is coherent and I would not oppose it, but it leaves the resulting prize resting on physiology alone. On the chair's question of whether the record supports Mojsov, I can only say that the committee has reason to keep her and that the dispute with Habener should be stated candidly in the discussion, not resolved by silence.

responses.point: Sandberg trimmed CAR-T to June and Sadelain because Rosenberg's adoptive cell transfer is a different achievement, and agreed that the omission of Knudsen should be recorded as a deliberate choice.
responses.response: I agree that the Knudsen omission should be recorded as deliberate, and I have done so above. On CAR-T I have moved toward his view. The engineered chimeric receptor with costimulation (June, Sadelain) is a coherent design achievement with durable remissions, while Rosenberg's cell therapy is a broader and earlier line of work, and Eshhar's original concept is not on the ballot. That is why I keep B030 as an alternative but would now support only June and Sadelain, not the trio, if it were ever used as a second part. It also reinforces my view that a two-part prize is not justified this year.

responses.point: Perlmann ranks the unfolded protein response (Walter and Mori) second as a clean, mechanistically complete pair, and says the optogenetic impact is mostly on how experiments are done, with medical benefit still prospective.
responses.response: I respect the compactness of the Walter and Mori pair and I ranked B040 fifth. El-Manira's point that Ron and Kaufman contributed the PERK and ATF6 branches makes the pair less clean than it looks, and the disease link is still mostly mechanistic with no therapy yet. On optogenetics I still think experimental impact counts for a Medicine prize, but I have to concede his and Wahren-Herlenius's allocation argument. No trio among Nagel, Hegemann, Deisseroth, Boyden, Bamberg and Miesenboeck avoids leaving out a decisive contributor, and I have therefore moved B012 from a plausible second part to an alternative I would use only if the record for B019 collapsed.

uncertainties: Whether the supplied record supports Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1 peptide over Habener's group, and if not whether Knudsen or a smaller group is the right third name.
Whether the committee wants the citation to recognise basic hormone discovery only or also to acknowledge long-acting analogue design without crediting it.
Whether a fair three-person group exists for optogenetics given Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenboeck.
Whether CAR-T credit should be limited to June and Sadelain, and how Eshhar's chimeric receptor concept should be treated.
statement.conflict_note: No documented tie to any credited name on the shortlist. My single-cell and spatial-transcriptomics work, and eight co-authored works with Rickard Sandberg, are unconnected to B019, B030 or B012. I request no recusal and no member has requested one.
